sections.h2: What the Pike County Recorder of Deeds does
sections.html:
The office records and indexes real estate documents for Pike County, such as deeds, mortgages and mortgage satisfactions. The same counter also collects realty transfer tax on behalf of the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, so the tax and the recording fee are paid together.

Find it at 506 Broad Street in Milford. Staff are there weekdays from 8:30 am to 4:30 pm, and the phone is 570-296-3508. Checks go to "Pike County Recorder of Deeds." A returned document carries a $10 return fee.

Recording comes last in a sale and decides whether the buyer's name shows up in the public index. A deed that sits in a drawer, or one that is rejected, leaves the seller on record as the owner, with consequences for property tax bills, liability and any lien searches that follow.

You can deliver the deed to the Milford office or send it through an electronic recording vendor. Two vendors serve title companies and law offices every day.

  • Simplifile, phone 800-460-5657
  • CSC, phone 866-652-0111
  • Walk it in or mail it to 506 Broad Street, Milford, PA 18337, with a check for the fee and, if the deed carries transfer tax, a payment for that

The fee schedule changes from time to time, so ask the office for the current deed fee before you write a check. A check in the wrong amount is one of the reasons a package comes back.

When a title company or attorney closes your sale, they normally prepare the deed, calculate the tax and file it. After closing, request the recording confirmation or book and page reference and keep it with your sale papers.

The recorder keeps a short checklist of defects. Most are clerical, and every one can be fixed before the deed leaves your hands.

  • The acknowledgment date falls before the date on the caption.
  • The acknowledgment leaves out the county, state, date, the names and titles of the people appearing, or the notary's signature, seal and expiration date. The office treats that acknowledgment as defective.
  • The deed leaves out the township, county or state where the property sits.
  • The amount written in words differs from the amount in numbers.
  • A document that refers back to an earlier mortgage omits that mortgage's book and page.
  • A set of papers for one transaction is not numbered in the order they should be recorded.
  • Property crossing two municipalities does not show the split of local transfer tax in dollars.
  • The deed lacks the grantee's address, or the grantee address is unsigned.
  • A foreign language document arrives without a written English translation.

If you are selling by yourself without a closing attorney, read this list against your deed line by line. The re-recording costs from a wrong document order fall on whoever submitted it.

sections.h2: Transfer tax on a Pike County sale
sections.html:
The state's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the value being transferred. Seller and buyer are jointly responsible, and the recorder takes it in along with any local tax.

Local transfer tax is the part that varies. Municipalities and school districts may add their own share, and Pike County deeds can cross municipal lines, which is why the recorder asks for the local split in dollars. Get the combined rate for your township or borough from the recorder before you sign a settlement sheet.

Some transfers pay nothing. The exemption list covers certain family transfers, transfers to governmental units and property that passes through an estate. If an heir later deeds the inherited house to a buyer, that second deed is an ordinary taxed sale.

sections.h2: Pike County housing at a glance
sections.html:
Pike County sits along the Delaware River at Pennsylvania's northeastern edge, with Milford as its seat and Matamoras as the largest borough. Many sales are in lake communities such as Saw Creek, Hemlock Farms, Pocono Woodland Lakes and Pine Ridge. The mid 2025 population is 62,808, up 7.3 percent from 2020, and the county has 40,861 homes.

  • Owner-occupied share of occupied homes: 87.0 percent
  • Typical owned home: $272,600 in value
  • Typical household income: $81,323
  • Typical gross rent: $1,378 a month

With owners living in 87 percent of occupied homes, a typical Pike County sale is an owner selling to another buyer rather than a landlord exiting a rental.

The recorder offers a fraud alert service through the county's online land records. Sign in at the Uslandrecords site, pick Pennsylvania and Pike County, register, and open the Alerts menu to get notice whenever a document is recorded under a name you pick. Setting up alerts does not need a credit card. Viewing or downloading images does.

An alert helps before and after a sale. Before closing, an alert under your own name shows whether anything unexpected gets recorded against your property. After closing, it confirms that your sale deed reached the index. Copies of recorded deeds are available by contacting the office or through the Property Record Search.

sections.h2: What should an heir or landlord do before selling?
sections.html:
Start with the title. When an owner has died, someone must be shown to have authority to sign for the estate. That is a matter for the Register of Wills and an attorney. The Recorder of Deeds only records what is presented.

Next, check for open mortgages. A mortgage that was paid off years ago may still look open in the index until its satisfaction is recorded, and the recorder's office files satisfactions as part of its normal work. A title company will want that cleared before closing.

Finally, think about timing. Tax bills, rent and repairs keep running while a deed waits for signatures. Someone who wants a quick closing can ask a buyer to take the house as it is. Even then, the deed is recorded the same way.

1. Before closing, confirm with the office or your title company the current deed fee and the local transfer tax rate for your township or borough.
  2. Check the deed against the defect list above, especially the acknowledgment, the grantee address and the match between words and numbers.
  3. Sign the deed before a notary, and check that the notary's seal and expiration date are filled in.
  4. The deed is filed either at 506 Broad Street or through Simplifile or CSC, with one payment for the fee and another for transfer tax.
  5. After recording, get the confirmation or the book and page reference and file it with your papers.

A sale for cash with no lender follows these same steps, though there is usually no mortgage satisfaction to track at the end.

faqs.q: Which office takes a deed for filing in Pike County?
faqs.a: The Recorder of Deeds at 506 Broad Street in Milford, or an electronic vendor. Simplifile and CSC handle online filing, and the counter keeps weekday hours.

faqs.q: What is the return fee on a rejected deed?
faqs.a: $10. The Pike County recorder charges that service fee on every returned document, so checking the acknowledgment and the amounts before you submit saves money and time.

faqs.q: Who is on the hook for transfer tax at a Pike County closing?
faqs.a: Both parties are liable together under state rules, though the sale contract usually assigns the cost. The state's share is 1 percent, and local taxes can add to it. The recorder can tell you the local amount.

faqs.q: Does inheriting a Pike County house trigger transfer tax?
faqs.a: No, title that passes through an estate is exempt. Selling afterward is a separate transfer, taxed like any other sale unless a different exemption fits.

faqs.q: How do I obtain a copy of a recorded Pike County deed?
faqs.a: Call the Recorder of Deeds at 570-296-3508 or use the Property Record Search on the county's land records site. Viewing or downloading images online requires registering a credit card.
